summary: Presents a practical framework for measuring end-to-end TCP throughput in a managed IP network, aiming to give a better sign of what users experience. It specifies TCP and IP parameters to optimize throughput testing.

eli5.summary: How fast is your internet really? This lays out a careful way for network operators to test how quickly data flows using TCP, so the result matches what customers feel.

subtitle: A practical method for measuring how fast TCP can really send data

tldr.problem: Network providers measure bandwidth at Layer 2/3 (individual packet speed), but this does not always predict the throughput that real applications experience. TCP is complex and depends on buffer sizes, latency, and network conditions. Providers need a way to measure actual TCP performance over their networks.
tldr.mechanism: This framework specifies a practical methodology for measuring TCP throughput in managed networks by identifying path MTU, measuring baseline RTT and bandwidth, and then conducting TCP throughput tests with specific metrics (transfer time ratio, efficiency, and buffer delay).
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now conduct repeatable, meaningful TCP tests that correlate with user experience. The framework defines three metrics to track TCP performance and provides guidance on interpreting results and investigating poor performance.

today: RFC 6349 is an Informational document describing a practical framework for TCP performance testing. It is widely used by network providers and enterprises to validate that managed networks can deliver promised TCP throughput. The framework has become a reference for service level agreement (SLA) testing and has informed the design of commercial TCP test equipment.

sections.title: Why TCP Throughput Testing Matters
sections.content:
Network providers typically guarantee bandwidth using Layer 2/3 metrics: the raw speed of the link, packet loss rate, latency, and jitter. These Layer 2/3 tests verify that the network hardware is functioning correctly. However, TCP throughput—the actual data rate that applications experience—depends on additional factors beyond raw bandwidth.

TCP uses a congestion window (CWND) at the sender and a receive window (RWND) at the receiver to limit the number of bytes in flight. These windows, combined with round-trip time (RTT), determine the maximum possible throughput. If either buffer is too small, TCP cannot achieve the guaranteed bandwidth even if the link is idle.

This framework provides a practical methodology for network operators to measure TCP throughput in managed, business-class IP networks. The goal is to verify that a network can actually deliver the promised bandwidth in terms that match user experience, not just raw hardware capacity.
sections.eli5: Testing internet speed with raw packets (pings and basic throughput tests) tells you if the wires are working, but TCP uses buffers and windows that can slow things down. This method tests the real TCP speed by setting up the buffers correctly and seeing how fast data actually flows.

sections.title: The Bandwidth-Delay Product and TCP Equilibrium
sections.content:
The Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) is the product of bottleneck bandwidth (BB) in bits per second and round-trip time (RTT) in seconds. It represents how many bits can be in flight on the network at any instant.

For example, a 100-Mbps link with a 5-millisecond RTT has a BDP of 100,000,000 bits per second × 0.005 seconds = 500,000 bits, or 62.5 KB. To achieve full throughput, a TCP connection must keep at least 62.5 KB of data in flight at all times. If either the send socket buffer or the receive window is smaller than the BDP, throughput will be limited.

TCP passes through three phases: Slow Start (exponential window growth at the beginning), Congestion Avoidance (linear window growth as TCP ramps up to find the maximum rate), and Loss Recovery (response when packet loss is detected). TCP Equilibrium is the steady state after congestion avoidance, where the TCP window has stabilized and TCP is sending at its maximum sustainable rate. This framework measures throughput only when TCP is in Equilibrium, because transient behavior during slow start and congestion avoidance does not reflect sustained performance.
sections.eli5: There's a number that describes how much data can be on the wire at once: bandwidth times delay. A 100-Mbps link with 5 ms latency needs at least 62.5 KB of buffer space. When TCP sets up its windows correctly and reaches a steady state, that's when you can measure true throughput.

sections.title: The Testing Procedure
sections.content:
The framework specifies three sequential steps.

Step 1: Identify the Path MTU. Use Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD) to find the maximum packet size that will transit the end-to-end path without fragmentation. Fragmentation slows TCP significantly, so knowing the correct MTU is essential.

Step 2: Baseline RTT and Bandwidth. Measure the round-trip time during off-peak hours (non-congested state) using either looped test equipment, packet captures, MIB statistics, or ICMP pings. Also measure the bottleneck bandwidth in both directions using stateless IP streams (not TCP) with techniques like those in RFC 5136. Calculate the BDP from these values to determine the required socket buffer sizes.

Step 3: Conduct TCP Throughput Tests. Using tools like iperf, run single or multiple TCP connection tests. For each test, measure three metrics: the TCP Transfer Time Ratio (actual time divided by ideal time based on the BDP), TCP Efficiency Percentage (the fraction of bytes that didn't need retransmission), and Buffer Delay Percentage (the increase in RTT during the test compared to baseline).

Tests should run for at least 30 seconds to properly exercise network buffers and should be conducted at different times of day. Both unidirectional (each direction separately) and bidirectional tests should be run.
sections.eli5: First, find the biggest packet that works. Then, measure the latency and speed when the network is quiet. Then, run real TCP transfers and measure whether they achieve the expected speed and how much data had to be resent. Do this in both directions and at different times.

sections.title: Metrics and Interpreting Results
sections.content:
The framework defines three metrics.

TCP Transfer Time Ratio: The actual time to transfer a block of data divided by the ideal time (calculated from the maximum achievable TCP throughput based on BDP). A ratio of 1.0 means the transfer was ideal. A ratio of 1.5 means the transfer took 50% longer than expected, indicating suboptimal performance.

TCP Efficiency Percentage: The percentage of bytes sent that didn't require retransmission. This is calculated as (Total Bytes Transmitted - Retransmitted Bytes) / Total Bytes Transmitted × 100. High efficiency (close to 100%) indicates low packet loss. Low efficiency indicates either network packet loss or RTT variability causing timeouts.

Buffer Delay Percentage: The increase in average RTT during the test compared to the baseline RTT, expressed as a percentage. This metric reveals whether the network is adding queuing delay, which increases latency for interactive applications.

Poor results can stem from several causes: network congestion causing packet loss (revealed by low efficiency), inadequate socket buffer sizes, incorrect TCP options configuration (window scaling, timestamps, selective acknowledgments), path MTU discovery failures, or issues with intermediate devices like firewalls or WAN accelerators that alter TCP parameters.
sections.eli5: Measure three things: how much longer the transfer took than expected (time ratio), how many bytes didn't need to be resent (efficiency), and how much the network slowed down compared to baseline (buffer delay). Together, these numbers tell you where the problem is if the test fails.

sections.title: Practical Considerations and Deployment
sections.content:
This methodology is designed for managed, business-class networks where network operators and customers have service level agreements. It assumes cooperation between network provider and customer because testing requires setting up test equipment at both ends of the path and may appear to network management tools as an attack.

The methodology does not apply to "best effort" internet access, because best-effort networks make no guarantees. Layer 2/3 tests (like RFC 2544) must be conducted first to verify the network is functioning correctly before running TCP tests.

When interpreting results, network operators and customers should understand that both ends of the TCP connection must be properly tuned. Modern operating systems like Linux, FreeBSD, Windows Vista and later, and Mac OS X 10.5 and later include automatic TCP window scaling and buffer tuning, which simplifies deployment. However, legacy systems may require manual configuration of socket buffers and TCP options.

For very high-bandwidth or very high-latency networks (Long Fat Networks), specialized test equipment is needed because standard computers may not be able to generate or receive TCP traffic at full link rate. Some organizations use dedicated communications test instruments (TCP TTDs) that can measure retransmissions and RTT variations with microsecond precision.
sections.eli5: This is mainly for business networks with service agreements. You need equipment at both ends, and both sides of the connection have to be configured correctly. Modern operating systems handle a lot automatically, but you may need special test gear for really fast or high-latency links.
